name: Zoe Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zoe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Does that sound all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'll answer straight, I'm not one for fancy words.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Hollis Electrical, a family firm in our market town, run by Mr Hollis and his son, and I'm the only junior. We do farm buildings, barns, village houses, the church hall, anything round the valley. I'm usually pulling armoured cable across a yard or wiring lights in a cold shed while Mr Hollis checks my work. I love that the farmers know us by name, and I hate the mud and the fact I'm still slow on the theory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. That's what Mr Hollis has said all along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Mr Hollis was right and the people selling it got carried away. I don't go online much, but at church I'd say it's a relief. I'd say good work still needs good people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, AI was never my worry. A family firm that took me on when nobody else would doesn't drop me over a gadget. What keeps me up is paying for a wedding on an apprentice's wage. Matt, my fiancé, and I have about 400 between us, and the wedding is in June.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down at Hollis and do every job they give me. I'd put my Saturday pay from the farm shop into the wedding fund. I'd ask my parents to help with the reception, which they've offered anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but about money, not machines. My job feels safe with the Hollis family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut from the wedding if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The band, probably, and the second dress for the evening. We'd keep the church and the meal at the village hall. My mum would do the flowers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your job feels safe. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Mr Hollis took me on after two other firms said no, and he's said he'll see me through my licence. That's a promise to him. In our town, people keep their word.

say: I'd say **Mr Hollis** was right that AI was overblown.
I'd tell people at **church** it's a relief that good work still needs people.
think: Hollis is a **family firm** that won't drop me over a gadget.
My real worry is paying for a **June wedding** on junior pay.
do: Do every job **Hollis Electrical** gives me without complaint.
Put Saturday **farm shop** pay into the wedding fund.
Ask my parents to help with the **reception**.
S0.quote: A family firm that took me on when nobody else would doesn't drop me over a gadget. What keeps me up is paying for a wedding on an apprentice's wage.
fieldNote: She trusts the **family firm's promise** more than any market trend.
Her pressure is a **wedding** on thin savings.
She leans on **parents and church** before anything public.

steps.text: Take every job Mr Hollis offers at the usual rate
Put Saturday farm shop pay into the wedding fund
Accept her parents' offer to pay for the reception

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first. Mr Hollis does his quotes on a notepad, so good luck to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine for offices, but country electrics are a different world. I'd say that to Matt and the lads at the farm shop. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I don't think it touches me much. A computer can write my boss's quotes. A computer can't climb into a cowshed roof in January and work out why the milking parlour keeps tripping. Maybe Mr Hollis's son would start using an app for quotes, and that's his business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, honestly. I'd wait and see what other firms do. If the Hollis son wanted me to use an app, I'd ask him to show me once and then probably forget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd still be thinking about the wedding more than any of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Matt's work in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Matt fixes tractors and farm machinery for a dealer. The new tractors already have computers in them, so he spends more time plugged into a laptop. He doesn't like it, but he's kept his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably forget the app. Is that a problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one day. But I'm not paid to sit on my phone, I'm paid to wire barns. If the Hollises need me on an app, they'll tell me.

say: I'd say AI is fine for offices, but **country electrics** are different.
I'd keep my view to **Matt** and the farm shop, not online.
think: A computer can't fault-find a **milking parlour** in a cowshed roof.
If the Hollis son uses an **app for quotes**, that's his business.
do: **Wait and see** what other firms do before changing anything.
Learn an app **once** if the Hollis son asks, then rely on him.
feel: Uneasy, but still thinking more about the **wedding** than AI.
S1.quote: A computer can write my boss's quotes. A computer can't climb into a cowshed roof in January and work out why the milking parlour keeps tripping.
fieldNote: She sees **rural hands-on work** as out of AI's reach.
Her fiancé's **tractor work** already has more screen time.
She leaves technology to **her bosses**, trusting them to decide.

steps.text: Wait and see what other valley firms do with AI
Keep wiring barns and sheds for Hollis Electrical

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. And robots by 2031. That's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is people playing God, and nobody voted for it. At church I'd say we need to look after each other. I wouldn't trust the government to fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd be in real trouble. If the robots come in 2031, my fiancé and I lose our trades within a few years of each other. We'd have a wedding and two sets of useless hands. Mr Hollis would keep me as long as he could, but if a robot can wire a barn, the farmers will buy the robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the wedding smaller and put the money towards rent. I'd stop the plan to buy a house and ask my parents if we can live with them for a few years. I'd lean on the church community for whatever work they know of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like the ground had gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Matt that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we get married anyway, smaller, and stay with my parents. Matt would want to keep the big plan, because he's stubborn. My mum would have the final say, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at any other kind of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what else I'd do. I'm not a computer person and I don't want to be. Maybe cleaning or care work, something that still needs a person.

say: I'd say this is people **playing God**, and nobody voted for it.
I'd say we need to **look after each other**, not wait for government.
think: Matt and I could lose our **trades** within the same few years.
If a robot can wire a barn, the **farmers will buy it**.
do: Make the **wedding smaller** and put the money towards rent.
Drop the house plan and live with **my parents**.
Ask the **church community** about any work going.
S2.quote: If the robots come in 2031, my fiancé and I lose our trades within a few years of each other. We'd have a wedding and two sets of useless hands.
fieldNote: She expects **both trades** in the household to go within a few years.
She distrusts government and turns to **family and church**.
She sees **no alternative path** besides low-paid caring work.

steps.text: Hold a smaller wedding in the village hall
Move in with her parents instead of buying a house
Ask the church community about local work
Put the wedding band money towards rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Robots in 2034. A bit longer, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's not panic. I'd say young people should learn a real trade properly, not rush into screens. Mr Hollis would say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be worried. Five years' warning wouldn't change what I do. I'd keep learning the trade properly, the way my boss learned it from his father. If there's no work at the end, at least I'll have done it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my licence with Mr Hollis. I'd keep the wedding as planned but save 20 a week after it for a house deposit. I'd wait and see what happens to bigger firms before I panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can live with it. There's time to get married and settle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it wouldn't change what you do. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Matt says I'm stubborn, and he's right. But I'd rather be good at one thing than half-good at five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most in the five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Hollis son taking over and changing everything. Mr Hollis is 63. His son is more modern and might bring in machines.

say: I'd say we've got **time**, so let's not panic.
I'd tell young people to learn a **real trade** properly.
think: Five years' warning **wouldn't change** what I do.
If there's no work at the end, at least I'll have **done it right**.
do: Keep the wedding as planned and then save **20 a week**.
**Wait** to see what happens to bigger firms.
feel: Anxious, but with time to **get married** and settle.
S3.quote: Five years' warning wouldn't change what I do. I'd keep learning the trade properly, the way my boss learned it from his father.
fieldNote: She openly admits she **wouldn't change** course with five years' warning.
The risk she sees is a **change of owner** at Hollis.

steps.text: Finish the licence under Mr Hollis
Save 20 a week for a house deposit after the wedding
Wait to see how bigger firms cope

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2039 for robots. I'd be about 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who works hard will be fine. At church I'd say trust in God and do your job well. I'd say the same to my younger brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still be a bit worried. Ten years is long enough to get my licence, get married and have a baby. Whether there's still work for me at 40 is in God's hands, not mine. I'd just keep doing what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my licence, get married and start a family in a few years. I'd keep working at Hollis and maybe take on more farm work when Mr Hollis retires. I'd save a little every month for the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in the background. Day to day, I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep doing what you're doing. Even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I know some would say that's foolish. But my grandfather kept the same job for 40 years and changes came and went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my future children to learn to do something with their hands and to look after each other. I wouldn't tell them to chase computers.

I'd tell my younger brother to **trust in God** and work well.
think: Ten years lets me get my **licence**, marry and have a baby.
Whether there's **work at 40** isn't in my control.
do: Stay at Hollis and take on more **farm work** when Mr Hollis retires.
Save a little each month for **future children**.
feel: Anxious in the **background**, fine day to day.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to get my licence, get married and have a baby. Whether there's still work for me at 40 is in God's hands, not mine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Matt and I would both lose our trades just as we're getting married. I don't want a government cheque. I want the family that taught me the trade to still have a trade to pass on. Helping small firms like Hollis keep going would mean more to me than any handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family firms. Big companies will buy robots, but small family firms are what keep the countryside working.

headlineQuote: I don't want a government cheque. I want the family that taught me the trade to still have a trade to pass on.
portrait: Zoe is a **27-year-old junior** at a family electrical firm wiring farms and village houses.
She **never uses AI** and trusts her boss's promise more than any trend.
Her calm-picture worry is paying for a **June wedding** on junior pay.
Fast AGI **alarms** her because she and fiancé Matt could both lose their trades.
Even with time she'd **keep going**, leaning on faith, family and church.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both her and Matt losing their trades as they marry.
whatWouldHelp: Support for **small family firms** to keep going, rather than handouts.
